components.text: The decisive demand is whether sinners justly deserve divine death and judgment rather than responsibility resting elsewhere.
The atonement account presupposes that the human beings receiving the penalty are properly responsible for the underlying sin.
Whether people justly deserve divinely imposed death and judgment for sin.
Whether guilt is straightforwardly attributable to the people whose penalty Christ allegedly pays.
The decisive demand is whether every person can justly deserve death and judgment for sin attributed to that person.
The payment analogy depends on guilty sinners actually owing the penalty that Christ allegedly pays.
Whether the sinners whose penalty is paid are personally and justly guilty.
Whether death and judgment are deserved by each person rather than inherited from predecessors.
The decisive demand is why Christ's penal payment is necessary or morally enabling if God controls judgment and forgiveness.
Why justice requires Christ to pay a penalty before God can forgive guilty people.
The decisive demand is whether avoidable divine world selection shifts responsibility for foreseeable sin from creatures to God.
The additional demand is whether inherited culpability is unjust because it is not grounded in the individual's acts.
Whether divine foreknowledge and avoidable world selection alter responsibility for sin.
Whether inherited guilt unjustly attributes predecessors' conduct to later people.
Whether a sovereign God could forgive without sacrificial payment.
The decisive demand concerns God's responsibility for knowingly selecting avoidable conditions producing sin and unbelief.
The additional demand concerns whether guilt can justly be inherited from prior human conduct.
Whether God's knowing and avoidable world choice changes responsibility attribution.
Whether guilt for predecessors' actions is morally attributable to later people.
Whether sacrificial payment is necessary for divine forgiveness.
The decisive demand is whether God's foreknown world choice displaces or undermines the individual's responsibility for serious wrongdoing.
The additional demand is whether original or inherited sin can justly ground personal guilt.
Whether original sin or inherited guilt can justly make a later person culpable.
Whether divine world selection displaces or changes personal responsibility.
Whether direct forgiveness is available without sacrifice.
The decisive demand is whether scripture and creation independently warrant God's existence and authority rather than presupposing them.
The additional demand is whether skeptical rejection is explained by culpable motive rather than inadequate evidence.
Whether scripture and creation independently establish God and warrant diagnosing denial as suppression.
Whether unbelief can be attributed to avoidance rather than evidential disagreement.
Whether the courtroom analogy can operate without first establishing God as judge.
The decisive demand is whether repentance and faith alone accurately state the gospel's conditions for obtaining eternal life.
Whether repentance and faith rather than works accurately state the conditions of eternal life.
The decisive demand is whether Jesus taught commandment keeping and relinquishing wealth as means of earning eternal life.
Whether Jesus taught commandment keeping and relinquishing wealth as ways to earn eternal life.
Whether the theological framework has independent evidential support.
The decisive demand is whether faith, scripture, and creation provide demonstrable grounds for God and divine authority.
The additional salvation claim relies on faith, but its central issue here is conditions rather than truth-tracking methodology.
Whether scripture and creation provide demonstrable warrant for God's existence and authority.
Whether rejection is culpable avoidance rather than evidential disagreement.
Whether the asserted salvation doctrine is independently warranted.
The decisive demand is whether religious faith and scripture reliably track truth when their foundational premises cannot be demonstrated.
A related earlier demand asks whether God bears responsibility for knowingly selecting a world containing suffering and sin.
Whether faith and scripture provide a sound method for reaching truth.
Whether using scripture to establish the framework is circular.
Whether a creator's world selection generates responsibility for foreseeable suffering.
The decisive demand is whether labeling creation fallen explains suffering without leaving the creator responsible for avoidable atrocities.
The additional demand is whether retained human guilt defeats the claim that God also bears responsibility.
Whether labeling creation fallen answers the creator's responsibility for foreseeable suffering and atrocities.
Whether personal wrongdoing excludes creator-level responsibility.
The decisive demand is whether third-party payment addresses wrongdoing rather than merely canceling the offender's liability.
A related demand is whether the salvation mechanism produces transformation rather than only declaring forgiveness.
Whether third-party payment addresses the underlying wrongdoing rather than only canceling its penalty.
Whether the salvation mechanism supplies transformation rather than only unearned release.
The decisive demand is why Christ's sacrifice permits or is needed for forgiveness rather than God forgiving directly.
The additional demand is whether substitution changes the offender's defective character rather than only removing liability.
Why sacrifice is needed before a sovereign God can forgive directly.
Whether substitution reforms the wrongdoer's defective character.
Whether the divine framework has independent evidential support.
The decisive demand is for truth-sensitive grounds supporting God, scripture, and resurrection beyond unsupported faith.
A related demand is for evidence independent of the divine and scriptural premises being asserted.
Whether there is a truth-tracking basis for believing the resurrection and related gospel premises.
Whether the case supplies grounds independent of scripture and presupposition.
Whether salvation reforms defective character.
The decisive demand is whether the promised repentance-and-trust test can fail in a way that counts against the promise.
The broader salvation claim promises a result from repentance and trust whose unsuccessful cases require explanation.
Whether the proposed repentance-and-trust test can independently confirm Christ and salvation.
Whether promised salvation has a testable and reliably operating mechanism.
Whether the stated faith-based route can accommodate sincere nonbelief after attempted compliance.
The decisive demand is whether a person or soul persists after bodily death so that postmortem judgment remains coherent.
A related demand concerns whether personal experience supports continued spiritual existence beyond brain-dependent identity.
Whether a persisting soul or self remains after bodily death to undergo judgment.
Whether the person can persist to receive eternal life after biological death.
Whether personal experience supports a separable enduring self.
